newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Apatit hopes to boost phosphate sales.
newsitem.headline: Apatit hopes to boost phosphate sales.

text.p: AO Apatit, Russia's largest extractor and processor of phosphorus ores, plans to boost exports of phosphates and is targeting markets in Latin America and South-East Asia, company officials said on Tuesday.

But they said the feasibility of the plan hinged on a project to deepen the Arctic sea port of Murmansk to allow bigger ships to load. Murmansk is just 200 kilometres (125 miles) from Apatity ore mines.
"The idea of deepening the sea bed near Murmansk has always been in the air," said Alexander Gorbachev, Director General of ZAO Apatit Trade.

He said work could start in October and last for up to a year. The project will be co-financed by Russia's Menatep group and the administration of the Murmansk sea port, but Gorbachev declined to say how much the project would cost.
"Ships loaded with our products usually have displacement of 25,000-30,000 tonnes and go to Europe," he said.
"Now we are looking at the possibility of loading ships of 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes to deliver phosphates to Brazil, Mexico, Canada, Austarlia and South East Asia."
He said Apatit was talking to firms in these countries about processing Russian phosphates into fertilisers.
Apatit, which describes itself as the world's third-biggest producer of phosphorus ores, supplied the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe of phosphates needed for mineral fertilisers.

But economic crisis in the former socialist states has reduced demand for fertilisers and Apatit expects to produce just 7.5 million tonnes of phosphates this year, down from 20 million tonnes in 1988.
"Markets in Latin America and South-East Asia...will prevent further falls of production," Gorbachev said. "This could be an excellent option because the sea off Murmansk never freezes."
He said Apatit wanted to oust traditional suppliers Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria from Latin American and Asian markets.
"Our phosphorus ores meet the highest world standards... Besides reserves are enough for at least another 100 years," Gorbachev said.
He said the project was promising because sea transportation is cheaper than railway transport within Russia. "It is cheaper to deliver our products overseas than within Russia."
Apatit will export from 1.6-1.8 million tonnes of phosphates from Murmansk this year and hopes to double this figure in some 5-7 years, if the project is implemented.
